      "answer": "Core histones are evolutionarily related to archaeal histones and several proteins involved in transcription, chromatin remodeling, and signaling. In the API’s current SCOPe release, 2.08, their classification is:\n\n• Family: H2A, H2B, H3, and H4 belong to “Nucleosome core histones,” a.22.1.1 (SUNID 47114). Separate families contain archaeal histones, a.22.1.2 (47129); “TBP-associated factors, TAFs,” a.22.1.3 (47134); and bacterial histone-fold proteins, a.22.1.4 (101318).\n• Superfamily: These families share the Histone-fold superfamily, a.22.1 (47113). This supports common evolutionary ancestry of their histone-fold domains, even when sequence similarity is weak. The TAF family includes histone-fold domains of TAF4 and TAF12, NF-YB and NF-YC, negative cofactor NC2 alpha and beta, CHRAC-14 and CHRAC-16, and Son of sevenless (SOS). Thus, its membership extends beyond proteins literally named TAF. Bacterial examples include Aq_328 and TTHA1479.\n• Fold: They share the Histone-fold, a.22 (47112), characterized by a three-helix core with a long central helix flanked by shorter helices. Sharing a fold alone establishes structural similarity, not necessarily homology; here, their shared superfamily provides the evolutionary inference.\n• Class: They belong to All alpha proteins, class a (46456). Class membership describes broad secondary-structure composition and does not establish ancestry.\n\nLinker histones H1/H5 require a separate answer: their globular domains belong to family a.4.5.13, within the winged-helix DNA-binding superfamily a.4.5 and DNA/RNA-binding 3-helical bundle fold a.4. Their superfamily relatives include forkhead DNA-binding domains and the DNA-binding domains of LexA and CAP. H1/H5 and core histones share class a, but SCOPe does not place them in the same fold or superfamily.\n\nThese relationships apply to classified domains, not automatically to entire multidomain proteins. For example, the histone-related domain of SOS does not make its catalytic domains histone homologues. Nor does shared ancestry imply that TAFs, NF-Y, NC2, CHRAC, or bacterial histone-fold proteins perform nucleosomal DNA packaging. Conversely, the term “histone-like” in bacterial proteins such as HU/IHF or H-NS describes functional resemblance and does not itself establish membership in the core-histone superfamily; histone-modifying enzymes are also not histone homologues merely because they act on histones. Specific function transfer requires independent biochemical and biological evidence. Structural templates should be selected using domain-level sequence alignment, coverage, structural quality, and assembly context; one histone structure cannot represent every family or interaction in this superfamily.",
